entry.title: PhD Applications Abroad: I Was Doing Everything Except the Right Things

PhD Applications Abroad: I Was Doing Everything Except the Right Things

When I started applying for PhD positions abroad during my master’s, I thought I was being serious about it.

I was not.

I had decided I wanted to go abroad — not just for research, but also for the kind of academic environment where people are more open to ideas and discussions. That part was clear to me.

What wasn’t clear was how the process actually works.

I didn’t know how to identify labs that genuinely matched my interests. I didn’t know how to write a proper first email. I didn’t know what a strong CV looked like in this context. And I definitely didn’t understand research papers well enough to talk about them with confidence.

So I did what felt like effort.

I wrote long emails to PIs.

Mistake: Writing long emails thinking it shows sincerity.

Very long emails.

I thought explaining everything in detail would show sincerity. In reality, it just made my emails harder to read. I was also hesitant to attach my CV in the first email — which, looking back, makes no sense. That is literally the one document that helps someone evaluate you quickly.

I was also filtering poorly.

Instead of being clear about which labs actually made sense for me, I would get interested in a lab, read a bit, and convince myself that this was “the one.” That kind of emotional attachment doesn’t help — it just biases your judgment.

The outcome was predictable.

No shortlists. Barely any replies. Mostly silence.

At that point, it’s easy to think:

“Maybe they don’t consider international applicants seriously.”

I thought that too.

But that wasn’t the real issue.

What Actually Changed

Two things shifted my approach.

First, I stopped focusing only on getting selected and started paying attention to the work itself.

There are people doing genuinely interesting research, and many of them are open to bringing in students who are willing to learn. That realization changed how I looked at labs — from places I need to get into to places where I could contribute.

Second, I got hands-on exposure through a project at CSIR.

Working on something real — writing drafts, analysing results — made it very obvious where I stood. It also made one thing clear: I had been thinking about applications without building enough clarity around my own work.

The Core Mistake

I delayed action because I was unsure.

I kept thinking I needed:

  • a better profile
  • more understanding
  • more confidence

before I could reach out properly.

Key Insight: Delay due to uncertainty is more damaging than rejection.

In reality, that delay just slowed everything down.

What I Would Do Differently

If I had to restart, I would simplify the process:

1. Fix the CV first

This is non-negotiable.

Your CV is the first filter. It should be clean, structured, and easy to scan. You don’t need to artificially inflate it with random certifications. Just present what you have properly.

Most people underestimate how much clarity in a CV matters.

2. Keep the first email short

You are not writing an SOP.

A good first email should:

  • clearly state your research interest
  • briefly connect it to their work
  • attach your CV

Mistake: Trying to impress instead of being clear.

That’s it.

If they’re interested, they’ll reply. If not, no amount of extra paragraphs would have changed that.

3. Don’t over-filter before acting

You don’t need the “perfect lab” before reaching out.

You need a reasonable match and a clear reason to contact them.

Overthinking this stage just delays useful feedback.

Final Thought

The biggest shift for me was simple:

Stop trying to feel ready. Start moving.

I spent close to a year doubting whether I was good enough to reach out properly. That hesitation cost me more than any rejection would have.

If you’re starting out, don’t repeat that.

Build your CV.
Write the short email.
Reach out.

You’ll learn more from a few ignored emails than from months of overthinking.
entry.summary: Lessons from applying without clarity — and what actually matters.

entry.title: Molecular Dynamics for Beginners: Watching Proteins Move (Step-by-Step)

link.title: Molecular Dynamics for Beginners: Watching Proteins Move (Step-by-Step)

entry.content:
If you understand basic biology but have never run a simulation, this is for you.

What are we actually doing?

A protein structure from PDB is a snapshot — like a photograph.

But in reality, proteins are not static. They:

  • fluctuate
  • breathe
  • change shape
  • interact with their environment

Molecular Dynamics (MD) tries to simulate this behavior using physics.

Think of it like this:

We take a protein and place it in a virtual environment, then let physics decide how it moves over time.

What you will actually learn

By the end, you will understand:

  • how a protein is prepared for simulation
  • why we add water and ions
  • what “running a simulation” really means
  • what kind of output you should expect

The big picture

Every MD simulation follows the same logic:

Clean structure → Add environment → Stabilize → Simulate

If you understand this pipeline, you understand MD at a practical level.

Step 1: Getting a protein

You start with a .pdb file.

Important point:

This structure is experimental, not perfect.

It may contain:

  • missing atoms
  • extra molecules
  • crystallization artifacts

So we don’t use it as-is.

Step 2: Cleaning the structure

We remove unnecessary components like:

  • water molecules (from crystal structure)
  • ligands (unless we specifically study them)

Why?

Because:

The water in a PDB file is not the same as the biological environment.

We will add our own controlled environment later.

fetch 1ABC
remove solvent
remove organic
save protein_clean.pdb, all

Step 3: Assigning a force field (topology)

This is one of the most important steps.

A force field defines:

  • how atoms interact
  • bond strengths
  • angles and charges

Without this:

The protein is just coordinates — it has no physics.

gmx pdb2gmx -f protein_clean.pdb -o processed.gro -water spce

This step essentially says:

“Here are the physical rules governing this system.”

Step 4: Putting the protein in a box

Why do we need a box?

Because simulations require boundaries.

We are not simulating an infinite space. Instead:

we simulate a small region and treat it as repeating.

gmx editconf -f processed.gro -o boxed.gro -c -d 1.0 -bt cubic

Biological meaning:

The protein now exists in a defined physical space.

Step 5: Adding water

Proteins function in aqueous environments.

Without water:

  • structure collapses
  • interactions become unrealistic
gmx solvate -cp boxed.gro -cs spc216.gro -o solvated.gro -p topol.top

Now:

the protein is surrounded by thousands of water molecules.

Step 6: Adding ions

Proteins often carry net charge.

If not corrected:

  • simulation becomes unstable
  • electrostatics become unrealistic
gmx grompp -f ions.mdp -c solvated.gro -p topol.top -o ions.tpr
gmx genion -s ions.tpr -o neutral.gro -p topol.top -pname NA -nname CL -neutral

Biologically:

we are approximating physiological ionic conditions.

Step 7: Energy minimization

Before simulation, we relax the system.

Why?

Because:

  • atoms may overlap
  • bonds may be strained

Energy minimization removes these issues.

gmx grompp -f minim.mdp -c neutral.gro -p topol.top -o em.tpr
gmx mdrun -v -deffnm em

If you skip this:

your simulation may crash or behave unrealistically.

Step 8: Running the simulation

Now we let physics evolve the system over time.

gmx grompp -f md.mdp -c em.gro -p topol.top -o md.tpr
gmx mdrun -deffnm md

What is happening here?

At each time step:

  • forces are calculated
  • positions are updated
  • the system evolves

This produces a trajectory — essentially a time-resolved dataset.

Step 9: What do you get?

You don’t just get a “video”.

You get:

  • atomic coordinates over time
  • energy values
  • structural changes

This allows analysis like:

  • RMSD (stability)
  • RMSF (flexibility)
  • binding behavior

What you just did (in simple terms)

You took:

  • a static protein

and turned it into:

  • a dynamic, physically realistic system

Common misunderstandings

  • MD is not “animation” — it is physics-based
  • Results are not automatically meaningful — they require analysis
  • Longer simulations are not always better without interpretation

What to do next

Once this workflow makes sense:

  • add a ligand (protein–drug system)
  • learn RMSD and RMSF
  • compare multiple simulations

Final thought

Don’t aim to understand everything immediately.

Run a simulation. Observe it. Then go back and understand each step.

That’s how most people actually learn MD.
entry.summary: A simple, beginner-friendly introduction to running your first MD simulation
